entry.title: Instructor Source Tour: How the Structured-Outputs Library Turns LLM JSON Into Pydantic Models

link.title: Instructor Source Tour: How the Structured-Outputs Library Turns LLM JSON Into Pydantic Models

entry.content:
If you have ever extracted structured data from an LLM, you have probably met Instructor: define a Pydantic model, hand it to client.chat.completions.create(response_model=...), and get back a validated, typed object instead of a string of JSON you have to scrape out of markdown fences yourself. The library sits on top of the OpenAI SDK and, through adapter functions, on top of Anthropic, Gemini, Cohere and a dozen other providers. Its README is disarmingly short, but the source has an architecture that rewards a closer look — especially now that the codebase has gone through a visible reorganization.

This post is a source tour of 567-labs/instructor at version 1.18.0 (the main branch as of this writing). The headline structural fact: the package you import, instructor, is now a thin facade. The historical modules under instructor/core/ have shrunk to three-line shims, and the real implementation lives in a v2 subtree — instructor/v2/core/ for the client and dispatch machinery, instructor/v2/providers/ for per-vendor handlers, and instructor/v2/dsl/ for the response-model helpers. Everything below links to the exact lines, verified against the tree.

The first diagram is the overview: the facade on the left, factories and the patch-and-dispatch core in the middle, the validation-and-retry loop on the right.

Overview of Instructor's request flow: the lazy-import facade feeds factory functions that build Instructor/AsyncInstructor wrappers around a patched create method; the patch layer consults the mode registry and delegates every call to the retry chain, where raw completions are parsed and validated into Pydantic models.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • instructor/__init__.py, L111 — the _LAZY_IMPORTS table. Importing instructor costs almost nothing; each public name (Instructor, from_openai, Mode, the DSL helpers) is resolved through a module-level __getattr__ the first time you touch it. Optional exports like from_anthropic are only added when the corresponding SDK is installed.
  • Instructor, L385 — the sync client wrapper. It stores the patched create_fn, the active Mode, the Provider, default kwargs and a Hooks registry, and exposes create, create_iterable, create_partial and create_with_completion.
  • AsyncInstructor, L758 — the async twin, overriding every create method with awaitable or async-generator variants.
  • from_openai, L119 — the factory that takes an openai.OpenAI (or compatible) client, patches its chat.completions.create, and returns an Instructor. The same file also powers from_anyscale, from_together, from_databricks and from_deepseek, because they are all OpenAI-wire-compatible.
  • from_provider, L92 — the string-based router: "openai/gpt-4o" or "anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet" is split on the slash, the right SDK is constructed, and the matching factory is called.
  • patch, L147 — the wrapper installer. patch_v2 (just above it, at L83) validates that the (provider, mode) pair is registered, then wraps the underlying callable in a sync or async shell.
  • ModeRegistry, L59 — the dispatch table. A dictionary keyed by (Provider, Mode) maps to a ModeHandlers bundle; lookups are lazily loaded under a lock, and the module-level singleton lives at L368.
  • retry_sync_v2, L138 — the validation loop. Every structured call passes through here: call the API, parse with the registry’s response_parser, and on a ValidationError or JSON error, hand the request to the registry’s reask_handler and try again.
  • process_response, L256 — the parsing dispatcher that turns a raw completion into a validated model and attaches the original response as _raw_response.

A Facade That Imports Nothing Until You Ask

The most interesting organizational decision in the current tree is how aggressively the package defers work. The top-level instructor/__init__.py declares __all__ and a _LAZY_IMPORTS dictionary — see L111 — and nothing else runs at import time except two small helpers. When you write instructor.from_provider(...), the __getattr__ hook imports .auto_client, which itself is a shim re-exporting instructor.v2.auto_client. The same pattern applies to Mode (a one-line re-export of instructor.v2.core.mode) and to the legacy instructor.core.client path, which is now a star re-export of the v2 implementation.

This buys two things. Cold-start time: importing instructor no longer drags in provider SDKs — Anthropic or Gemini are only imported when their factory is resolved, and only if the SDK is installed, as the _add_optional_export calls at the bottom of __init__.py show. Backward compatibility: older code doing from instructor.core.patch import patch keeps working through the shims. The cost is indirection — a stack-trace frame pointing at instructor/core/retry.py is really executing code in instructor/v2/core/retry.py.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is a single package; there is no separate “provider pack” to install for the common case:

pip install instructor
# or: uv add instructor / poetry add instructor

The core dependencies, per pyproject.toml, are openai, pydantic (2.8+), tenacity, httpx and jinja2, and the library supports Python 3.9 through 3.x (anything below 4.0). If you plan to use Anthropic or Gemini factories, you install those SDKs yourself; Instructor detects their presence at import time.

The canonical first program, straight from the README:

import instructor
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int


client = instructor.from_provider("openai/gpt-4o-mini")
user = client.chat.completions.create(
    response_model=User,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "John is 25 years old"}],
)
print(user)  # User(name='John', age=25)

What actually happens on that last call: from_provider constructs the OpenAI client and calls from_openai, L119, which returns an Instructor whose create_fn is the patched chat.completions.create. The chat and completions attributes on the wrapper are literally self — properties at L474–484 of the client — so the call site reads like vanilla OpenAI while the patched function does the schema work. If you want the raw completion too (token counts, finish reason), call create_with_completion instead; the wrapper returns a (model, raw_response) tuple, implemented at L708. Retry behavior is controlled by max_retries (default 3) on the create signature at L538.

patch() and the Mode Registry

The heart of the library is the pair patch / patch_v2 in instructor/v2/core/patch.py. patch accepts either an OpenAI-style client or a bare create callable, resolves the underlying method, and hands it to patch_v2, which consults the registry and returns a wrapper. The sync wrapper — _create_sync_wrapper, L185 — is where the per-request choreography happens:

  1. Reject response models containing async validators (the sync path cannot honor them).
  2. Validate any token_budget against the request via the budget helpers in instructor/v2/core/budget.py.
  3. Pop cache kwargs — the wrapper supports transparent response caching when a cache adapter is passed.
  4. Look up the ModeHandlers bundle from the registry and call its request_handler to inject provider-specific fields — for Mode.TOOLS, the tools array built from your model’s openai_schema; for JSON modes, the schema folded into the system message. The schema itself is generated by generate_openai_schema, L26 from your Pydantic model (docstring included as the description).
  5. Run message templating (handle_templating) so Jinja-style placeholders in messages can be filled from a context dict.
  6. Check the cache for a hit, then enter the retry chain with an isolated copy of the messages so reask mutations cannot leak into caller state.

The Mode enum in instructor/v2/core/mode.py, L10 enumerates roughly forty strategies: TOOLS, TOOLS_STRICT, JSON_SCHEMA, RESPONSES_TOOLS, and vendor-specific entries like ANTHROPIC_TOOLS, GEMINI_JSON, CEREBRAS_TOOLS. Each has an entry in the registry whose bundle is typed by ModeHandlers, L47: a request_handler, a reask_handler, a response_parser, and optional streaming extractors and message converters. The contract those handlers implement is the abstract ModeHandler, L17, whose prepare_request and handle_reask methods define how a request is dressed up and how a failed attempt is rebuilt.

The Validation Loop: Parse, Reask, Repeat

Once the prepared request reaches retry_sync_v2, L138, the code builds a tenacity Retrying policy — stop_after_attempt(max_retries + 1), optionally combined with stop_after_delay when a timeout is set — and enters the loop. On each attempt it emits the completion:kwargs hook, calls the real API, emits completion:response, and accumulates token usage into a running total via update_total_usage, L117, which understands both OpenAI’s CompletionUsage and Anthropic’s Usage objects. That total later shows up on your model instance as _total_usage.

If the model parses and validates, the loop returns immediately, attaching _raw_response (and, for list results, a ListResponse wrapper — instructor/v2/dsl/response_list.py, L15). If instead the parser raises a ValidationError, a json.JSONDecodeError, an AsyncValidationError or a ResponseParsingError — the tuple of retryable errors is defined at the top of the retry module — the failed attempt is recorded as a FailedAttempt, the parse:error hook fires, and the registry’s reask_handler rebuilds the request. For tools mode that job belongs to reask_tools, L161 and its siblings: they append the validation error to the conversation, then raise to trigger the next attempt. When attempts run out, the loop raises InstructorRetryException, L188, carrying the last completion, the attempt count, the accumulated usage and the full FailedAttempt history for debugging.

The detail diagram traces this machinery end to end, including the pieces the overview compresses:

Detail view: facade shims, the client layer with hooks, patching-layer request preparation (templating, budget, caching), the (Provider, Mode) registry contract, the retry chain with usage accumulation and reask handlers, and the DSL types process_response understands.

The Response DSL

Not every response is a single flat model, so instructor/v2/dsl/ provides a small family of wrappers. Partial[User] — the Partial factory, L599 — builds an all-Optional mirror of your model so streamed chunks can be parsed as they arrive; the README’s streaming example prints a User whose fields fill in one by one. IterableModel — defined at L204 of iterable.py — wraps a tasks list schema so one completion can yield many validated objects, with IterableBase supplying the chunk-splitting machinery. ModelAdapter, L32 lets you pass a bare Python type like str or list[int] as the response model, and CitationMixin (L5) adds quote-anchored citations to any model. Under the hood, tool-call models ride on ResponseSchema, L119, whose openai_schema class property (at L124) produces the function-calling schema and whose from_response delegates straight back into the registry parser.

If you build tool-facing systems, the schema-generation half of this story pairs naturally with the MCP Python SDK, where tools also declare typed input schemas; for model-quality measurement rather than structure, see lm-eval-harness. For agentic retrieval flows that overlap with Instructor’s extraction niche, see our LlamaIndex source tour.

Honest Limits

Staying within what the project itself claims: the README positions Instructor as a structured-extraction tool and explicitly says so — “Use Instructor for fast extraction, reach for PydanticAI when you need agents” — and its comparison section argues it is “focused on one thing — structured extraction” relative to agent frameworks. Popularity claims on the README (3M+ monthly downloads, 10K+ GitHub stars) are the maintainers’ own figures, not ours. We did not run any benchmarks for this post and none are implied.

A few limits are visible in the code itself. The sync create path rejects async validators rather than honoring them, by design. apatch is a deprecated alias that emits a DeprecationWarning (patch.py, L171), and Mode.FUNCTIONS prints a deprecation warning when selected (client.py, L407) — the library is steering users toward tools modes. The v1-to-v2 reorganization means some documentation and code paths disagree about module locations; reading instructor/core/*.py shims before instructor/v2/core/ is the fastest way to avoid confusion. Finally, retries are only as good as the model’s willingness to fix its own output: the reask handlers feed validation errors back verbatim, which works well for schema slips and helps less with models that persistently misunderstand the task.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of 567-labs/instructor: the lazy-import facade, the patch() wrapper, the (Provider, Mode) handler registry, and the tenacity-driven validation loop that reasks the model until the JSON fits.

entry.title: LlamaIndex Source Tour: How the Data Framework for LLM Apps Is Assembled

link.title: LlamaIndex Source Tour: How the Data Framework for LLM Apps Is Assembled

entry.content:
Ask a room of Python developers how they wire private documents into large language models, and sooner or later the answer will be LlamaIndex. The run-llama/llama_index repository is the home of that framework: a data layer that connects files, APIs, and databases to LLM prompts through indexing and retrieval. The README describes it as a “data framework” that offers connectors to ingest your existing data sources, ways to structure that data into indices, and an advanced retrieval and query interface that turns raw sources into knowledge-augmented output.

This post is a source tour, not a usage tutorial. We read the current main branch of the repository end to end, traced the classes that make up llama-index-core, and verified every symbol and line number below directly against the code before publishing. Two diagrams anchor the discussion: a compact overview of the moving parts, and a larger detail map that adds the retrieval stack, response synthesis, and storage internals.

The architecture is deliberately modular: reading, chunking, indexing, retrieval, and answer synthesis each live in their own module with little glue between them. Once you know the seams, you can swap any component — a different LLM, a different vector store, a different chunking strategy — without disturbing the rest. That swap-friendly design is why hundreds of integration packages coexist around a single core.

LlamaIndex overview: documents flow from SimpleDirectoryReader through SentenceSplitter into VectorStoreIndex, while Settings configures the LLM and embedding model used by the query flow.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SimpleDirectoryReader, L208 is the default entry point for local files; its load_data() method at L718 turns a folder of PDFs, markdown, and docs into Document objects.
  • TextNode, L765 is the universal currency of the framework: everything that gets embedded, stored, retrieved, and cited is a node, and Document at L1097 is just the top-level node that wraps a whole source file.
  • SentenceSplitter, L34 chunks documents into nodes; its split_text() at L176 respects sentence boundaries while keeping chunks inside a token budget.
  • BaseIndex, L25 defines the index contract — from_documents() at L89, insert() at L229, and factory methods that hand back engines and retrievers.
  • VectorStoreIndex, L36 is the flagship implementation; its constructor resolves the embedding model from Settings, L291, the module-level global every component falls back to.
  • RetrieverQueryEngine, L25 closes the loop on the query side: its _query() at L203 retrieves nodes and hands them to a response synthesizer backed by BaseLLM, L27.
  • StorageContext, L53 sits under everything, bundling the docstore, index store, and vector store that give the index somewhere to live.

The full detail map

The overview hides how much choice lives inside each box. The detail diagram below opens them up: the node data model, the retriever family, the synthesizer hierarchy, and the storage layer, all with the exact classes you will meet in the code.

Detail map of llama-index-core — every node links back to the real class in the repository, grouped by responsibility.

Two Packages, One Namespace

LlamaIndex ships in two shapes. The llama-index starter package bundles core plus a selection of integrations for people who want to be productive immediately. The llama-index-core package contains only the engine, and you add exactly the integration packages your application needs — the README counts over three hundred of them on the integrations page. The import system makes the split visible: statements that include core come from the core package, and statements without core come from an integration. The README’s own example is from llama_index.core.llms import LLM for the abstraction and from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI for a concrete provider.

This namespace rule is more than a style choice; it is the dependency direction of the whole ecosystem. Integrations subclass the abstract bases in core — BaseLLM, L27 with chat() at L89 and complete() at L113, or BaseEmbedding, L72 with get_text_embedding() at L385 — and core code only ever references the abstract interfaces. That is what keeps a vector store swap or an LLM swap a one-line change at the application level.

The coordination point is the Settings object at L291 of settings.py. It is a module-level singleton that remembers your default LLM, default embedding model, default tokenizer, and default transformations. Every component that needs a model but was not given one explicitly asks Settings first. This is why the README quickstart works with no configuration: unset components resolve to defaults that make sense for the installed starter package.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s recommended path for a customized setup is plain pip:

pip install llama-index-core
pip install llama-index-llms-openai
pip install llama-index-llms-ollama
pip install llama-index-embeddings-huggingface

The minimal example from the README then builds a vector index in four lines of Python:

import os
os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "YOUR_OPENAI_API_KEY"

from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader

documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("YOUR_DATA_DIRECTORY").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)

Under the hood, from_documents() — the classmethod at L89 of indices/base.py — runs the reader output through the default transformation list, which chunks each document with the sentence splitter, and then embeds the resulting nodes into the vector store held by a freshly built StorageContext.

If you would rather keep everything local, the README shows the Ollama configuration. You assign onto Settings directly:

from llama_index.core import Settings, VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader
from llama_index.embeddings.huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbedding
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

Settings.llm = Ollama(model="llama-3.1:latest", request_timeout=360.0)
Settings.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"
)
Settings.embed_model = HuggingFaceEmbedding(model_name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")

documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("YOUR_DATA_DIRECTORY").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)

Setting the tokenizer matters more than it looks: the sentence splitter measures chunk sizes in tokens, so if the tokenizer does not match the model, your chunks are measured with the wrong ruler. The tokenizer side of this story — vocabulary files and model-agnostic counting — is the same machinery behind libraries like HuggingFace tokenizers, and the transformers package supplying AutoTokenizer is covered in our transformers source tour.

Querying is symmetric in simplicity:

query_engine = index.as_query_engine()
query_engine.query("YOUR_QUESTION")

And persistence is a one-liner each way, straight from the README:

index.storage_context.persist()

from llama_index.core import StorageContext, load_index_from_storage
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(persist_dir="./storage")
index = load_index_from_storage(storage_context)

The Index Layer: BaseIndex and Its Heirs

BaseIndex is an abstract generic class that fixes the lifecycle every index follows: documents go in through from_documents() or incremental insert(), nodes flow through a transformation list, an index-specific struct gets built, and the class exposes as_query_engine() at L491 and as_retriever() at L489 as the public exits.

VectorStoreIndex is the implementation most people meet first. Three details in its source are worth noticing. First, its constructor immediately resolves the embedding model with resolve_embed_model(embed_model or Settings.embed_model) — explicit arguments beat globals, and globals beat nothing. Second, _build_index_from_nodes() at L260 embeds nodes in configurable batches (insert_batch_size defaults to 2048), so large corpora do not build one giant request. Third, as_retriever() at L112 lazily imports and returns a VectorIndexRetriever, L24, which performs top-k similarity search against whatever vector store the index was built on.

The base class also offers from_vector_store() at L87, which wraps an existing vector store that already contains your text — useful when an external service owns the data. For non-vector strategies, SummaryIndex, L29 keeps all nodes in a flat list and retrieves the whole corpus or filtered subsets, which suits summarization-style queries where everything might be relevant. Indices are also reloadable: load_index_from_storage() at L12 rebuilds the right index class from a persisted storage context.

Query Execution: Retrievers, Engines, and Synthesizers

A query travels through three small stages, each with its own abstract base. The unit of input is QueryBundle, L1449, which wraps the raw query string plus an optional embedding vector, and the unit of output is NodeWithScore, L1035, which pairs a node with a relevance score.

The retrieval stage is BaseRetriever, L34. Its public retrieve() at L192 handles callbacks and normalization, then dispatches to the private _retrieve() at L263 that subclasses implement. The retriever family is where LlamaIndex’s research surface lives: AutoMergingRetriever, L26 merges small chunk hits back into larger parent chunks, QueryFusionRetriever, L33 fans a query out over multiple retrievers and fuses the ranked results, RecursiveRetriever, L22 follows node relationships to pull in referenced material, and RouterRetriever, L20 delegates to one candidate chosen by a selector.

The synthesis stage is where the answer gets written. as_query_engine() wires the index’s retriever together with a synthesizer produced by get_response_synthesizer() at L38, the factory behind the ResponseMode enum. The default mode builds a CompactAndRefine, L13, which extends Refine, L196. Refinement is simple and effective: the LLM drafts an answer from the first compact batch of chunks, then each subsequent batch updates that draft. Refine.get_response() at L599 drives the loop, packing retrieved text as densely as the context window allows before spending model calls. The whole engine is thin: RetrieverQueryEngine._query() is essentially retrieve-then-synthesize, with BaseQueryEngine.query() as the sync entry and an async twin beside it.

Storage and Persistence

By default, everything lives in memory. The README is explicit about this, and the defaults confirm it: a fresh StorageContext at L53 holds a SimpleDocumentStore, L20 for nodes, a SimpleVectorStore, L64 for embeddings, and an index store — all plain dictionaries. SimpleVectorStore.add() at L174 appends vectors to a dict, and its similarity query() at L244 does a brute-force cosine comparison.

StorageContext.from_defaults() at L74 is the assembly point: pass it a vector store, docstore, or persist directory and it wires the right combination together. Its persist() at L151 writes each store under ./storage, which is what index.storage_context.persist() reaches through the index. Swapping in a production vector store is therefore a matter of constructing a different StorageContext — the index code never knows the difference. One more ingestion-time convenience: IngestionCache at L17 records transformed nodes so repeated ingestion runs can skip documents whose content hash has not changed.

Honest Limits

The README itself is candid that the project’s center of gravity has moved. The current focus, it says, is building an AI-powered engine for document parsing and extraction, with LlamaParse as the commercial platform and liteparse as the open-source parser; the OSS framework remains available but is no longer the primary focus. Judge recent commit activity accordingly.

A few other limits worth internalizing before you build on it. The “over 300 integration packages” figure is the README’s own count — we did not audit it. Default storage is in-memory, so a process restart without persist() discards your vectors. The quickstart path assumes an OpenAI key by default, and the local Ollama path requires you to manually align the tokenizer with your model — get that wrong and chunk sizes are silently mismeasured. On packaging, the wheel ships an _static folder containing nltk and tiktoken caches; the README documents a GitHub attestation procedure for verifying those build assets in restricted environments. Finally, the project’s own ParseBench and ExtractBench cover parsing and extraction quality, not RAG accuracy — we found no framework-level retrieval benchmarks in the README, and we decline to invent any.

Related reading on the model side of the stack: our transformers source tour, the tokenizer internals behind tokenizers, and weight serialization in safetensors.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the llama_index repository: ingestion, indices, retrievers, response synthesis, and storage inside llama-index-core.

entry.title: Inside LM Evaluation Harness: How EleutherAI Turns a Model and a YAML File into a Benchmark Score

link.title: Inside LM Evaluation Harness: How EleutherAI Turns a Model and a YAML File into a Benchmark Score

entry.content:
Every benchmark leaderboard you have seen — MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K — is computed by software that has to make hundreds of small, boring decisions correctly: how the prompt is assembled, how many few-shot examples are drawn and from which split, how the model’s answer is extracted from raw generated text, and how per-sample numbers collapse into one headline figure. For open models, that software is often the LM Evaluation Harness from EleutherAI — the framework behind the Open LLM Leaderboard lineage and the de facto reference for reproducible LLM scoring.

The library has a reputation for being “just YAML”, and the YAML surface is real — the lm_eval/tasks directory on the main branch contains roughly fourteen thousand task configuration files. But underneath that declarative skin sits a compact, elegant runtime: an evaluator core that walks every task, a request abstraction that turns documents into four kinds of scoring jobs, a set of model adapters that all answer the same two verbs, and a metric/filter layer that converts free-form text into numbers. This post walks that runtime from the command line down to the token logits, with every symbol linked to the actual source at the commit we read.

We will follow one thread the whole way: what exactly happens between lm_eval --model hf --tasks mmlu --limit 100 and a JSON file full of accuracies. If you evaluate models for a living — or you are building your own harness and want to steal the good ideas — this is the map.

Overview of the harness on the main branch: the CLI funnels into simple_evaluate, which loads YAML tasks through TaskManager, turns documents into Instance requests via ConfigurableTask, dispatches them to a backend such as HFLM or VLLM, and scores the filtered responses with the metric registry.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli_evaluate, L5 is the console entry point; it builds a HarnessCLI, L10 parser whose run subcommand (Run, L18) translates flags into a library call.
  • simple_evaluate, L55 is the one-call orchestrator: it fixes all four random seeds, resolves the model string through the registry, wraps the model in CachingLM, L275 if you asked for response caching, and overrides per-task settings like num_fewshot.
  • TaskManager, L37 maintains a cached TaskIndex, L36 over the YAML forest and its load method (L179) resolves names, tags, and inline dicts into live task objects via TaskFactory, L25.
  • ConfigurableTask, L618 is the workhorse: one Python class that interprets a TaskConfig, L82 dataclass — dataset path, splits, doc_to_text, metric_list, filter_list — and implements the whole lifecycle declared in the abstract Task, L64.
  • ContextSampler, L17 draws the few-shot examples for fewshot_context, L933, with FirstNSampler, L104 and BalancedSampler, L117 as deterministic and per-label alternatives.
  • evaluate, L429 is the request loop: after build_all_requests, L268 fills each task with Instance, L11 objects, it groups them by request type and executes resps = getattr(lm, reqtype)(cloned_reqs) at L600 — the request type literally is a method name on the model.
  • On the way out, RegexFilter, L16 extracts answers from generated text, and process_results, L1455 computes per-sample metrics that the aggregation registry — for instance mean, L35 — collapses into the final score.

From Install to Your First Model

The package installs as lm_eval (the CLI alias is the same name), and the fastest smoke test uses a tiny checkpoint:

pip install lm-eval
lm_eval --model hf --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-70m \
  --tasks hellaswag --limit 100 --batch_size 8

Three things happen that are worth understanding before you scale up. First, the model string hf is not a class import; it is a registry key. The module lm_eval/models/__init__.py registers every known adapter alias lazily in _register_all_models, L66, and simple_evaluate resolves it with get_model, L613 — which is also how third-party packages plug in backends through entry points. Second, --model_args pretrained=... is parsed into a dict and passed to the adapter constructor, so the flags you pass are just keyword arguments of HFLM.__init__. Third, the task name hellaswag goes through the task index, which maps the name to a YAML file; the YAML in turn names the datasets split and the prompt template. Nothing about HellaSwag is hard-coded — it is all configuration, which is why the community has contributed thousands of tasks.

The same call also demonstrates the reproducibility contract: simple_evaluate sets separate seeds for Python’s random, numpy, torch, and the few-shot sampler, then records all of them, plus the git hash and environment info, into the results object (EvalResults, L19). If two runs disagree, the JSON tells you what differed.

How a Task Becomes a Request

The heart of the design is a four-value enum of request types, declared in lm_eval/api/instance.py: loglikelihood, loglikelihood_rolling, generate_until, and multiple_choice. Every benchmark reduces to one of these verbs: a classification benchmark is multiple_choice (argmax over choice likelihoods), open-ended generation is generate_until, and perplexity benchmarks use the rolling variant.

ConfigurableTask.construct_requests (L1362) shows how far one method can stretch. For multiple_choice it builds one loglikelihood request per choice, gluing the target delimiter onto each continuation; if the task requested acc_mutual_info, it additionally builds unconditional (empty context, choice) pairs so the score can be normalized by the choice’s unconditional probability. For generate_until it attaches a deep copy of the task’s generation_kwargs so per-task sampling settings cannot bleed into each other. The resulting Instance dataclasses — request type, source document, arguments, and later the responses — are cached as a whole by build_all_requests through load_from_cache, L53, keyed by task, shot count, rank, and chat-template settings.

The few-shot context itself is assembled in fewshot_context, L933, which builds a message list: optional system instruction plus the task description, then num_fewshot examples drawn by the sampler (which removes the current evaluation document from its own draw), then the evaluation document without its answer. If apply_chat_template is set, the same message list is rendered through the tokenizer’s chat template — with fewshot_as_multiturn deciding whether prior examples become separate user/assistant turns or one concatenated user message.

The detailed view adds the internals: CLI subcommands, the evaluator's helpers and result schema, the task index/factory/index machinery, the samplers, the LM → TemplateLM → HFLM/VLLM/TemplateAPI adapter hierarchy, the filter ensemble, and the logging layer.

Backends: Swap Without Rewrites

All model adapters implement the same narrow interface declared in LM, L25: answer loglikelihood and generate_until batches, expose rank/world_size for distributed runs. A shared base class, TemplateLM, L356, owns the tokenization boilerplate — most importantly _encode_pair, L393, which encodes context and continuation, moves trailing whitespace into the continuation to preserve word-boundary tokenization, and splits the whole-sequence encoding to get exact continuation token IDs. Get this function wrong and every likelihood benchmark silently changes meaning; the harness gets it right once, in one place.

The default adapter, HFLM, L62, wraps the Transformers library directly. Its scoring path batches requests, runs one forward pass, and slices the continuation logits; its generation path _model_generate, L1153 defaults the temperature to 0.0 and, unless you explicitly set do_sample, strips the temperature and runs greedy decoding with custom stop-sequence criteria. Determinism is the default; sampling is opt-in.

For throughput, the VLLM, L59 adapter swaps in vLLM as the engine. The trick: scoring does not change conceptually — _model_generate, L388 issues a request with SamplingParams(temperature=0, prompt_logprobs=1, max_tokens=1, detokenize=False) — one forward pass per prompt with log probabilities enabled — which reproduces HFLM’s likelihood numbers at vLLM’s batched speed. The adapter also handles tensor-parallel serving, Ray-based data-parallel replication, and optional LoRA adapters. If your model is served behind an HTTP endpoint instead, TemplateAPI, L105 speaks to any JSON API — including TGI deployments and OpenAI-compatible servers — with a pluggable payload template, retry logic in model_call, L453, and an async path with semaphore-based concurrency.

Scoring: Filters, Metrics, Aggregation

Generation tasks produce prose; metrics want values, and the harness splits that problem in two: filters clean the raw text, metrics score the cleaned text. A task’s YAML lists any number of filter chains in filter_list, and ConfigurableTask builds each one at init time via build_filter_ensemble, L11, which looks components up in the filter registry and wraps them in a FilterEnsemble, L34. The most-used component is RegexFilter, L16 — its default pattern, #### (\-?[0-9\.\,]+), is a giveaway that it was born for GSM8K-style answers — and when nothing matches it returns the fallback [invalid] rather than crashing. MultiChoiceRegexFilter, L123 instead picks the answer choice that appears in the response. Each filter chain produces its own filtered_resps bucket, so one run can report exact-match under two extraction rules simultaneously.

Metrics themselves are registered, not imported: register_metric, L707 attaches to each metric name its aggregation function, output types, and direction (higher_is_better), and task YAML just names the metrics. process_results computes raw per-sample values — for multiple_choice that means the argmax over choice log-likelihoods, plus byte- and character-length-normalized variants for the well-known acc_norm — and the evaluator collects them into per-metric lists. At the end, _process_results, L375 applies the registered aggregation (exact_match_hf_evaluate, L234 under a mean, perplexity as exp(-mean(loglikelihood))), bootstraps standard errors, and folds task scores upward through ConfigurableGroup, L346 nodes so that an umbrella benchmark like mmlu aggregates from its subtasks with the weighting its YAML specifies. Results and samples stream out through the tracker (EvaluationTracker, L123) and optionally to WandbLogger, L24.

Distributed correctness gets real attention: when world_size > 1, evaluate pads each rank’s request list so every rank performs an equal number of forward passes, runs a barrier after each request type, and gathers metrics and logged samples to rank 0 before aggregation.

Honest Limits

The YAML surface is a strength and a liability. Fourteen thousand configuration files are maintained by hand, and their sheer number makes review hard; task definitions drift, near-identical benchmarks get duplicated under different names, and prompt-format choices that matter enormously for scores stay invisible unless you read the file.

Extraction brittleness is the second caveat. RegexFilter’s fallback [invalid] keeps a run alive when the model rambles, but every such sample silently becomes a wrong answer for exact-match metrics. A model that answers correctly but in an unexpected format gets punished for formatting, not reasoning — and with chat-template variants this makes cross-paper score comparisons genuinely unsafe unless the template settings match.

Third, the multiple-choice normalization heuristics (acc_norm dividing by character length, the byte-length variant) are exactly that — heuristics with known failure modes on short-choice tasks. And the distributed padding logic carries its own in-code caveat: it pads per request type and does not account for tasks that mix request types within one document. Nothing here invalidates the numbers, but these are decisions the harness makes on your behalf, and the only defense is knowing they exist.

Finally, defaults encode opinions worth re-checking: bootstrap_iters=100000 for stderr costs time on big runs, and predict_only bypasses metrics entirely. And no harness can save you from contamination between a model’s pretraining data and a public benchmark — that is a property of the corpus, not the tool. Use it as a measurement instrument, read the task YAML for anything you publish, and treat cross-model comparisons as valid only when the shot counts, templates, and filter chains match. Within those rules, it remains the most trustworthy open scoring tool the ecosystem has — and reading its source, as we did here, is the fastest way to internalize what a benchmark score actually measures.

entry.title: Marqo Source Tour: Inside the AI-Native Vector Search Engine’s Architecture

link.title: Marqo Source Tour: Inside the AI-Native Vector Search Engine’s Architecture

entry.content:
Marqo is an open-source vector search engine with a simple pitch: you hand it documents — text, images, or mixed content — and it generates embeddings for you, stores them, and lets you query them in natural language through a single REST call. Instead of bolting an embedding model onto a separate vector database yourself, Marqo treats “which model embeds my data” as an index setting and handles the whole flow, from media download and preprocessing to ANN ranking, inside one system. This tour walks the actual source of marqo-ai/marqo at branch mainline (version 2.26.2, per components/common/src/marqo_common/version.py), and every symbol below is linked to the exact line I read.

The deployment shape is the first thing that surprised me. Marqo is not a single Python process: the repository is split into four Python components under components/ — the main API server (marqo), an inference orchestrator (inference_orchestrator), a model management container (model_management), and shared code (common). The root compose.yaml wires those together with NVIDIA Triton Inference Server and expects a Vespa node reachable on the host. Ports tell the story: the API listens on 8882 (uvicorn.run(app, host="localhost", port=8882) in components/marqo/src/marqo/tensor_search/api.py), model management on 8883, the orchestrator on 8884, and Triton on 8000/8001/8002. Embeddings never happen in the API process — they are shipped over HTTP to the orchestrator, which drives Triton over gRPC.

Underneath it all sits Vespa as the storage engine. The VespaClient in components/marqo/src/marqo/vespa/vespa_client.py is the only thing that talks to it: YQL queries in, document feeds out, application packages deployed when schemas change. Marqo’s “index” is really a generated Vespa application — schema files rendered from Jinja templates — which is why index creation is a heavyweight operation in this codebase. If you have followed my earlier posts on USEARCH or pgvector, you will notice the opposite design philosophy: those tools are minimal storage engines you drive yourself, while Marqo owns the full stack from model to index.

Marqo overview: the FastAPI server (left) wires core services through Config; documents and queries flow through the Vespa store (bottom), while every embedding request detours to the inference orchestrator and Triton (right). Click any node to open the source on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • app = FastAPI(...), L111 — the API entrypoint that mounts every route: create index, add documents, search, embed, recommend, model management, and health.
  • generate_config(), L51 — runs once at import time and builds the three remote clients: VespaClient, InferenceClient, and ModelManagerClient, then wraps them in a Config.
  • Config, L22 — the wiring hub; its constructor instantiates IndexManagement, Monitoring, Document, Recommender, Embed, and Typeahead, each receiving exactly the dependencies it needs.
  • IndexManagement, L29 — owns index lifecycle: create_index at L128 generates and deploys a Vespa application package; get_index at L588 reads settings back.
  • Document.add_documents, L44 — the bulk add entrypoint; it picks one of three index-specific handlers and lets that handler vectorise and feed documents.
  • tensor_search.search, L324 — the root search method; validates limits, fetches cached index settings, then dispatches by searchMethod (TENSOR by default).
  • InferenceClient.vectorise, L31 — every embedding, whether from indexing or querying, leaves the API process through this HTTP call to the orchestrator’s POST /vectorise handler at L88 of components/inference_orchestrator/src/inference_orchestrator/main.py.
  • VespaClient, L40 — pooled HTTP client with query at L279 and feed_batch_multithreaded at L421; also handles Vespa application deployment at L95.
  • HybridSearch, L64 — runs the tensor and lexical legs together and merges their result sets when searchMethod=HYBRID.

The Detail View

The detail diagram zooms into the six functional areas the overview hides: the API layer, the Config-wired core services, the search core, the Vespa store adapters, the Marqo-side inference client, and the two sidecar services.

Detail view: from generate_config down to Triton gRPC calls. Three Vespa index adapters — structured, semi-structured, and unstructured — show how one backend serves three index flavours.

Two things in this view deserve attention. First, MarqoCustomRoute in components/marqo/src/marqo/api/route.py (L9) is a custom FastAPI route class that logs full stack traces before re-raising, and api.py registers a large ordered exception-mapping table (L137–180) that converts core, Vespa, and inference exceptions into consistent HTTP responses. Second, CachingInference (L14 in caching_inference.py) is a decorator around InferenceClient: when MARQO_API_INFERENCE_CACHE_SIZE is greater than zero, repeated content skips the network round trip entirely, backed by pluggable LRU/LFU caches.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest smoke test, straight from components/marqo/src/marqo/README.md, is a single container: docker run --name marqo -p 8882:8882 marqoai/marqo:latest. That image bundles enough of the stack to serve requests on port 8882, and http://localhost:8882/docs exposes the live Swagger UI generated from the FastAPI app (the README also shows how to pull the raw openapi.json).

For a real run you want the full component stack from the repo. Start a Vespa container (docker run --detach --name vespa --publish 8080:8080 --publish 19071:19071 vespaengine/vespa:latest), deploy Marqo’s local application package to it with the prepareandactivate curl documented in the developer guide, and then bring up the Python side with docker compose -f compose.yaml up, which starts Triton, the API, model management, and the orchestrator with the right environment variables — VESPA_CONFIG_URL, VESPA_QUERY_URL, VESPA_DOCUMENT_URL all point at host.docker.internal, and MARQO_REMOTE_INFERENCE_URL points at the orchestrator. Developers who want breakpoints can skip the API container entirely and run uvicorn api:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8882 from src/marqo/tensor_search, as the README’s Option B describes.

Your first index is one POST against a verified route (@app.post("/indexes/{index_name}"), L315 of api.py):

curl -X POST http://localhost:8882/indexes/my-first-index \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tensorFields": ["description"]}'

IndexSettings in components/marqo/src/marqo/tensor_search/models/index_settings.py defaults to a semi-structured index with model hf/e5-base-v2 (L27), so the minimal body is enough — Marqo will download and load that HuggingFace model on first use. Adding documents hits the /documents route (L550), whose AddDocsBodyParams accepts a documents list of plain dicts (components/marqo/src/marqo/api/models/add_docs_objects.py):

curl -X POST http://localhost:8882/indexes/my-first-index/documents \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"documents": [{"_id": "post-1", "description": "A short tutorial about vector search"}]}'

Then search — the SearchQuery model (models/api_models.py L42) defaults to searchMethod: TENSOR and limit: 10:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8882/indexes/my-first-index/search \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"q": "embeddings tutorial"}'

The first search may feel slow while the model loads into Triton, but after that, query embeddings are cached and the ANN search itself is Vespa’s job.

How a Search Query Travels

tensor_search.search (L324) is the root of the tree. It validates limits (MARQO_MAX_SEARCH_LIMIT, MARQO_MAX_SEARCH_OFFSET, and friends), then pulls the index definition through index_meta_cache.get_index (L44 of index_meta_cache.py), an in-process cache with a background refresh thread so hot searches do not re-read settings from Vespa. Dispatch then branches on searchMethod: _vector_text_search (L1124) embeds the query text through the inference client and asks Vespa for nearest neighbours; _lexical_search (L558) builds a keyword query instead; and HybridSearch.search (L65) executes both and merges. The Marqo-to-Vespa translation happens in the index adapters — StructuredVespaIndex builds tensor, lexical, and hybrid YQL queries (to_vespa_tensor_query at L419 of structured_vespa_index.py) — and VespaClient.query (L279) executes them. Highlights come back out of the response in _extract_highlights (L1030).

There is also a query-free recommendation path: the /recommend endpoint (L492 of api.py) calls Recommender.recommend (L199 of recommender.py), which fetches stored vectors for seed document IDs, interpolates them, and searches — the docstring is explicit that no inference happens during this process.

The Bulk Add Path

The ingestion flow is the more interesting half of the system. After the API parses AddDocsBodyParams, Document.add_documents (L44) reads the index definition and instantiates exactly one of three handlers: StructuredAddDocumentsHandler, SemiStructuredAddDocumentsHandler, or UnstructuredAddDocumentsHandler (L57–66 of document.py). They share a base class, AddDocumentsHandler (L107 of core/vespa_index/add_documents_handler.py), whose add_documents (L127) runs a fixed sequence: validate every document, infer modality per tensor field, convert the batch into Vespa documents (_convert_to_vespa_docs, L246), vectorise tensor fields through the inference client (_vectorise_tensor_fields, L283), and finally feed everything with VespaClient.feed_batch_multithreaded (L421). Failures are collected per document rather than failing the whole batch, and the response reports errors indexed by original list position.

Media handling is delegated to the orchestrator side: when treatUrlsAndPointersAsMedia is set, the API sends URLs and the orchestrator’s media_download_and_preprocess service downloads images or video and chunks them before embedding. Text fields go through configurable chunking too — IndexSettings defaults to sentence-based splits (index_settings.py L32–36). Partial updates use a separate PATCH route (L572 of api.py) and VespaClient.update_documents_batch (L601), so re-embedding is avoided when only non-tensor fields change.

Index Types and Schema Generation

Creating an index is where Marqo shows its Vespa inheritance. IndexManagement.create_index (L128) renders a VespaApplicationPackage (class at L593 of vespa_application_package.py) — schemas generated from .sd.jinja2 templates plus the services definition — and deploys it through VespaClient.deploy_application (L95). For clustered setups, a Zookeeper-backed distributed lock (_vespa_deployment_lock, L709) serialises deployments, and Config._connect_to_zookeeper (L69 of config.py) degrades gracefully to a warning if Zookeeper is unreachable. The three index types trade flexibility for schema stability: structured indexes predeclare every field, semi-structured (the default, L20 of index_settings.py) adapts the schema as new field counts grow, and unstructured indexes keep the old dynamic-mapping behaviour. ANN tuning is exposed up front: HNSW with efConstruction=512, m=16, and prenormalised angular distance (L49–55).

Honest Limits

Start with the headline: the project README states that Marqo’s open-source project is deprecated and will no longer receive updates, pointing commercial users to the managed platform at marqo.ai. The mainline branch remains a fascinating read and a working system, but plan for maintenance being on you. The second limit is weight: a full stack is five containers plus Vespa’s JVM, and index creation triggers real deployments — if you want an embedded engine that lives inside your process, my earlier notes on USEARCH or pgvector cover that end of the spectrum. Third, inference is always remote in this architecture: the API has no in-process embedding fallback, so a broken orchestrator or Triton takes embeddings down with it, and model loading is governed by MARQO_MODELS_TO_PRELOAD and the model management container. Finally, as wired in compose.yaml, the HTTP surface has no authentication layer — only telemetry middleware is registered (L118–119 of api.py) — so it is meant to sit inside a trusted network. Model coverage is nonetheless a genuine strength: the registry resolves HuggingFace transformers checkpoints such as the default hf/e5-base-v2, CLIP-family vision-language models through OpenCLIP, and ONNX-friendly setups behind Triton.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of marqo-ai/marqo: how the FastAPI server, Vespa vector store, and Triton-powered inference sidecars wire together into one vector search engine.

entry.title: OpenAI Evals: A Source Tour of the LLM Evaluation Framework

link.title: OpenAI Evals: A Source Tour of the LLM Evaluation Framework

entry.content:
Every serious LLM project eventually hits the same wall: you changed one word in a prompt, or swapped one model checkpoint for another, and you have no idea whether the output got better or worse. OpenAI’s answer is evals, the Python framework behind the company’s own model evaluations. It is more than a folder of test cases — it is a small operating system for evaluation: a YAML-driven registry that turns names into Python classes, abstract base classes that define what an eval is, a protocol that abstracts “call the model” behind a single callable, and a recorder that streams every event into an auditable JSONL log. Here we walk that path through the actual code on main, from the moment you type oaieval to the moment a final report lands in a log file.

Two design decisions make this codebase worth studying even if you never run it. First, everything is resolved by name strings: an eval id like test-match maps to a YAML entry, which maps to a class path like evals.elsuite.basic.match:Match, imported and instantiated at runtime — the indirection that lets contributors add evaluations without touching the runner. Second, the framework separates what is evaluated (the Eval) from how the model is reached (a CompletionFn) and how results are stored (a Recorder). If you have read our tour of the community sibling lm-eval-harness, you will notice the opposite emphasis there: a giant task table and metrics library, where evals centralizes the plumbing instead.

The tour below uses two diagrams generated from the repository graph — the first gives the lay of the land, the second drills into one run. Every symbol and line number mentioned was verified against a sparse checkout of openai/evals at main.

The openai/evals overview: the oaieval CLI resolves specs from the Registry, drives the Eval base class over CompletionFn implementations, while every event flows into the Recorder. The elsuite library supplies concrete evals.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The entry point is the oaieval console script, wired in pyproject.toml to run, L118, which resolves the eval, builds a RunSpec, L75, and drives one evaluation.
  • The Registry, L103 lazily loads YAML directories — evals, solvers, completion fns, eval sets — via _load_registry, L287 and resolves names through get_eval, L210.
  • Spec objects are plain pydantic dataclasses in evals/base.py: EvalSpec, L51 carries the cls string and args; RunSpec, L75 mints a unique run_id in __post_init__, L85.
  • The abstract Eval, L46 class defines the sample loop; its threaded fan-out lives in eval_all_samples, L112.
  • Model access is abstracted by the CompletionFn, L23 protocol, implemented for OpenAI endpoints by OpenAICompletionFn, L83 and OpenAIChatCompletionFn, L134.
  • Every observation becomes an Event, L44 appended by RecorderBase, L54 and flushed to JSONL by LocalRecorder, L316.
  • Concrete evals live under evals/elsuite/: Match, L9 for exact scoring and ModelBasedClassify, L14 for model-graded judgment.

The Registry: YAML In, Python Classes Out

The registry is the framework’s address book. Its constructor takes a list of paths — by default the in-repo evals/registry directory plus ~/.evals, per DEFAULT_PATHS, L30 — and each resource type (evals, solvers, completion fns, eval sets, modelgraded specs) is a subdirectory of YAML files. Loading is deferred: the _evals and sibling collections are functools.cached_property descriptors, so the YAML parses once, on first access, in _evals, L325. Each entry gets its key, its source file’s basename as group, and any class: key renamed to cls — all inside _load_registry, L287, which also rejects duplicate ids and reserved keywords.

Name resolution is the clever part. A registry entry may be a plain string or a dict containing an id, which is just an alias for another entry; _dereference, L156 follows that alias chain until it lands on a real spec, then constructs the typed dataclass. When the CLI asks for an eval that does not exist, the error message is genuinely helpful: difflib.get_close_matches suggests the nearest five ids. Class instantiation happens later via make_object, invoked from get_class, L153, which imports module:Class strings like evals.elsuite.basic.match:Match and injects the spec’s args.

The same machinery serves models. make_completion_fn, L120 recognizes three kinds of names: the literal dummy (a canned DummyCompletionFn, L48 — invaluable for testing without spending tokens), a chat model id like gpt-3.5-turbo detected by is_chat_model, L83, or anything else, looked up as a completion-fn or solver spec and instantiated. Context windows come from a hard-coded table in n_ctx_from_model_name, L37 — a snapshot whose comment honestly dates itself: “Model list last updated 2023-10-24.”

The Detail Map: One Run, End to End

The detail map follows one run: oaieval resolves the eval spec through the registry, the Eval base class fans samples over a thread pool, each sample calls a CompletionFn or a Solver, and match, sampling, and metric events stream into the recorder's JSONL log.

Eval, SolverEval, and the Sample Loop

evals/eval.py defines the contract every evaluation implements. The docstring on Eval, L46 is candid: a subclass overrides two methods — eval_sample, abstract at eval_sample, L77, and run, abstract at run, L86. The constructor takes the resolved completion functions, a registry path, a seed (default 20220722), and the eval’s dotted name, which must have at least a base_eval.split shape.

The fan-out is where the framework earns its keep. _index_samples, L30 shuffles sample indices with a fixed SHUFFLE_SEED of 123 — so runs are comparable even when the caller’s seed changes — and honors a global cap set by set_max_samples, L41 from the CLI’s --max_samples flag. Then eval_all_samples, L112 maps work items over a ThreadPool sized by EVALS_THREADS (default 10), or runs sequentially under EVALS_SEQUENTIAL. Per sample, it binds f"{base}.{split}.{idx}" as a sample id and enters as_default_recorder, L90, a context manager exposing the recorder and sample id through contextvars — which is why deep inside a completion function you can call the module-level record_sampling and it lands in the right place. Samples load via get_jsonl, L120, resolved against the registry’s data directory.

The newer sibling SolverEval, L168 inverts the model: instead of calling a completion function per prompt, it evaluates a Solver, L41 — an agent-like object that receives a TaskState, L24 with a task description, message history, and arbitrary state. SolverEval deep-copies the solver per sample so stateful solvers cannot contaminate each other, and via EVALS_GENTLE_INTERRUPT a Ctrl-C still reports metrics over the samples already finished.

Scoring primitives live in evals/api.py. record_and_check_match, L55 implements the workhorse pattern: prefix-match the sampled text against the expected option(s), require a separator after the prefix if one is defined, and record a match event with expected, picked, and sampled fields. Aggregation happens in evals/metrics.py: get_accuracy, L12 averages the correct flags of match events, while get_bootstrap_accuracy_std, L21 resamples half the events a thousand times to estimate the error bar next to every accuracy number.

CompletionFns, Solvers, and Prompt Formatting

The CompletionFn, L23 protocol is deliberately tiny: a callable taking a prompt (a string or a list of role/content messages) and returning a CompletionResult with get_completions(). The concrete OpenAI implementations wrap the openai client with a hand-rolled retry loop — OPENAI_TIMEOUT_EXCEPTIONS at L19 lists rate limits, connection errors, timeouts, and server errors, and both openai_completion_create_retrying, L27 and openai_chat_completion_create_retrying, L41 retry through it. After each call they record a sampling event including the raw usage, which the CLI later sums into per-run token counts.

Prompt formatting is its own small module. evals/prompt/base.py defines two type aliases — OpenAICreatePrompt, L15 for legacy completions and OpenAICreateChatPrompt, L19 for chat messages — plus two adapter dataclasses: CompletionPrompt, L86 renders a chat log down to User: / Assistant: prefixed text via chat_prompt_to_text_prompt, L22, and ChatCompletionPrompt, L103 lifts a plain string into a single system message. One eval body can thus serve both text-davinci-003-era and chat-era models without branching. Multiple-choice harnesses also get make_abc, L8 for shuffled A) B) C) option strings.

Solvers extend the protocol toward agents. Solver, L41 subclasses CompletionFn (so the registry treats both uniformly) and implements __call__ to deepcopy the task state, run the abstract _solve, then chain any configured PostProcessors — Strip, L5 and friends — over the output, recording each transformation. Composition is handled by NestedSolver, L137, which validates sub-solver specs and caches instances, plus recipes like CoTSolver, L9 and provider solvers such as OpenAISolver, L22. This is the natural seam for tool-using agents: a solver that calls tools shaped like the mcp-python-sdk contract plugs in without changing the eval that grades it.

Model-graded evals — where one model judges another — tie the stack together. ModelBasedClassify, L14 fetches a ModelGradedSpec, L12 from the registry (choice strings, input/output mappings, a prompt template), generates the completions under test, and asks the last completion function in the list to classify them; metaeval mode even grades the grader. Because these evals are pure YAML plus a shared class, the README notes this is currently the only contribution path — custom-code evals are not being accepted.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps setup short: pip install -e . from a clone (Python 3.9 minimum), or pip install evals if you only want to run existing evals, with OPENAI_API_KEY exported beforehand. One gotcha: the sample datasets under evals/registry/data use Git-LFS, so a fresh clone shows pointer files until you run git lfs fetch --all; git lfs pull.

Your first run then needs two positional arguments — a completion function name and an eval name — as declared by get_parser, L25:

oaieval gpt-3.5-turbo test-match

That resolves test-match through the registry, instantiates Match, and writes a JSONL log to the default path /tmp/evallogs/{run_id}_{model}_{eval}.jsonl unless --record_path overrides it. Flags worth knowing: --max_samples 20 for a cheap smoke test, --dry_run to swap in the console-only DummyRecorder, --registry_path for your own YAML, and --extra_eval_params for per-eval settings like num_few_shot. The recorder choice is made in build_recorder, L242: local JSONL by default, an HttpRecorder posting batched events under --http-run, or the Snowflake-backed Recorder for OpenAI-internal dashboards. When the run ends, the CLI prints the final report and add_token_usage_to_result, L269 folds summed token counts into it. For suites, oaievalset expands an eval-set YAML into oaieval subprocess commands with checkpointed resume, driven from run, L81.

Honest Limits

Three facts from the README frame your expectations. First, the README’s opening banner points you to configure and run evals “directly in the OpenAI Dashboard” — the project’s center of gravity has moved to a hosted product, and the team is currently not accepting evals with custom code; only model-graded YAML contributions are reviewed. Second, several pillars are frozen in time: the registry’s context-window table is annotated as last updated 2023-10-24, and the completion functions target the openai client of that era — bring your own CompletionFn (the protocol makes that a small class) for newer endpoints or local servers. Third, the Snowflake recorder and its environment variables exist for OpenAI’s internal use; external users realistically use the local JSONL path — the format is just newline-delimited Event dicts with a spec header and a final_report trailer.

None of that diminishes the framework’s value as a blueprint. The registry’s name-to-class indirection, the sample-id-scoped recorder context, and the CompletionFn seam are patterns you can lift into any evaluation stack — including the community harness compared in lm-eval-harness. And the lineage runs deep: many registry datasets still reference completions from the gpt-2 era, when “evaluation” meant perplexity and exact match.
